newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq denies reports it arrests, kills Turkomans.
newsitem.headline: Iraq denies reports it arrests, kills Turkomans.

text.p: BAGHDAD, Sept 7 (Rueter) - Iraq on Saturday strongly denied reports that it had arrested and killed Turkomans after Iraqi troops stormed the main city of Arbil in the country's north to help one Kurdish faction fighting a rival Kurdish group.

"We stress that these rumours and news are prepared by parties who have wicked political purposes...they are baseless," said the Iraqi News Agency, quoting a Ministry of Culture and Information spokesman.

"All know that the Iraqi armed forces...had liberated the city of Arbil and protected Iraq's land from Iranian interference...and as soon as they completed their mission they pulled back," the spokesman said.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, in her latest round of consultations with the U.S. ambassador on events in neighbouring Iraq, on Saturday demanded Western protection for ethnic Turks in northern Iraq.

Iraqi opposition sources and representatives of the Turkomans, a Turkic community of around two million of whom 200,000 live in northern Iraq, have said Iraqi soldiers were arresting and killing some Turkomans after troops captured Arbil in a joint attack with an Iraqi Kurdish faction a week ago.
Officials of the Iraqi Turkoman party in Ankara have said around 2,000 Turkomans are missing from Arbil since the attack.
"It is known that it is not within these (Iraqi) troops' mission to carry out security tasks in the city (Arbil) or other cities," the Iraqi spokesman said.
Ciller, referring to U.S.-led air patrols over northern Iraq set up after the 1991 Gulf War to protect Iraqi Kurds, said in Ankara the Turkomans should be protected under the air operation.

"Under Operation Provide Comfort it was envisaged that Kurdish citizens in northern Iraq be protected. We want the Turkomans to be taken within this framework of protection," Tansu Ciller told reporters after meeting ambassador Marc Grossman.

Washington has said it launched 44 cruise missile strikes against southern Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday in retaliation for Baghdad's military assault in Arbil, severly damaged Iraqi air defence and destroying up to 11 of 15 targets.

Iraq said on Saturday that its air defence units fired surface-to-air missile against the U.S. and allied planes policing allied-established no-fly zones in northern and southern Iraq but added the missiles missed the targets.

Hummadi, a former Iraqi culture and information minister, blamed Washington for pushing Ankara into trying to impose the security zone. Ankara proposed the temporary zone last week and Washington said it had nothing against the idea.
"The Turkish government move is prompted by the American government not by the Turkish interest," Hummadi said.

His comments were made during a protest in front of the U.N. office in Baghdad, along with Iraq's speaker of the Assembly Sadoon Hammadi and several members of parliament, against last week's U.S. missile strikes against Iraq.
"If the Turkish government insists on that buffer zone and interfering in Iraq's internal affairs, we think it will not be in the interest of both countries (Iraq and Turkey)," he added.
